scope_justification: To regulate a feedback system's output by combining proportional, integral, and derivative actions on the error signal, achieving fast response, zero steady-state error, and disturbance rejection.
People made the tracheostomy tube to maintain a surgical airway below the larynx for patients whose upper airway cannot be kept open, so that long-term ventilation and suctioning are possible.

Engineers built it to eliminate steady-state error in feedback control systems by accumulating past error over time and applying a corrective output proportional to the accumulated integral, so that constant offsets in process variables are driven to zero even in the presence of unmeasured disturbances and model mismatch.
Signal processing mathematicians needed a family of orthogonal sequences with optimal spectral concentration for minimizing spectral leakage in finite-duration signals.

People made the main-bronchus construct to map the two primary airway trunks branching from the tracheal carina into each lung, so that surgeons can access the right and left lungs separately during thoracic procedures.
To express matrix constraints as convex feasibility problems in control design and optimization
People made the lobe construct to map each named division of a lung cut off by its interlobar fissures, so that surgeons can plan lobectomy and radiologists can localize disease to a named lobe.

People made the laryngeal inlet construct to map and categorize the opening into the larynx from the pharynx, so that clinicians can identify its landmarks during intubation and recognize its boundaries in head and neck surgery.

People created ISTFT to reconstruct time-domain signals from their short-time Fourier transform representation, enabling phase recovery and signal synthesis in audio processing and speech applications.

To simultaneously improve a feedback system transient response and steady-state accuracy using a single compensator network with both phase-lead and phase-lag sections, parameterized by crossover frequency, phase-lag center frequency, and attenuation factors for each section.
To implement state-space control when not all states are directly measurable, by combining a state estimator with a state-feedback law into a single dynamic compensator.

People made the lobar bronchus construct to map each named airway branch that enters a specific lung lobe through the pulmonary hilum, so that thoracic surgeons can isolate individual lobes during lobectomy and radiologists can localize lobar consolidations.
To compute the state-feedback gain matrix for single-input systems via the dual of the Ackermann formula formulation using the observability matrix and polynomial coefficient differences.

A human-made computational artifact needed to bridge time-domain signals to frequency-domain analysis — the complex-valued outputs that encode amplitude and phase information at each frequency component.

People made the cough reflex construct to map the coordinated neurophysiological sequence that clears the airway of irritants, so that pulmonologists and neurologists can diagnose and treat pathological cough syndromes.
To quantify the maximum amplification in a closed-loop system's frequency response, so designers can assess relative stability and predict time-domain ringing.

A nonlinear state estimation algorithm that represents the posterior distribution as a set of weighted samples (particles) propagated through the nonlinear dynamics, enabling arbitrary non-Gaussian inference for complex multimodal systems.

People made the pulmonary-lobule construct to partition each lung lobe into small pyramidal units bounded by connective tissue septa, so that pathologists can localize disease to a discrete structural unit and radiologists can interpret septal patterns on CT.

People made the quadrangular membrane construct to map the fibrous sheet spanning the laryngeal inlet that suspends its margins, so that laryngologists and surgeons can orient the vestibule, the ventricle, and the inlet during endoscopy and surgery.

People made the external-laryngeal-nerve construct to map the motor branch of the superior laryngeal nerve that innervates the cricothyroid muscle, so that surgeons can preserve it during thyroidectomy and neck dissection.
To characterize the response speed of a first-order system by specifying its characteristic time parameter tau, the time at which the step response reaches 63.2% of steady-state.

People made the palatopharyngeus muscle construct to map the longitudinal pharyngeal muscle that elevates the pharynx from the soft palate origin so that clinicians can assess swallowing function, evaluate velopharyngeal disorders, and plan palatal surgery.

People made the middle-pharyngeal-constrictor construct to map the intermediate pharyngeal constrictor muscle band arising from the hyoid apparatus, enabling clinicians to assess swallowing mechanics and pharyngeal wall abnormalities.
To identify the frequency at which a feedback loop's phase reaches -180 degrees, the point at which the gain margin is read and instability risk is evaluated.

To provide a systematic procedure for designing state-feedback controllers by selecting gain matrices that place closed-loop poles at desired locations, ensuring stability and performance specifications are met.

People made the laryngeal ventricle construct to map and categorize the hourglass-shaped space between the vocal folds and vestibular folds within the larynx, so that clinicians can identify its boundaries during endoscopy and recognize pathological distension.

People made the arytenoid cartilage construct to map and categorize the paired pyramidal cartilages at the posterior larynx, so that clinicians can identify their role as the attachment point for vocal fold muscles and recognize pathology during laryngeal surgery.
Neuroscientists and seismologists needed a spectral estimation method with controlled bias-variance trade-off for noisy, short-record signals.
To quantify how sensitive a feedback system's closed-loop behavior is to perturbations in the plant or controller, providing the central robustness metric for control design.
People made the airway category to name the whole air passage as a single functional unit, so that clinicians can manage, clear, and protect it across the organs that line it.
To quantify how heavily a second-order system's oscillation is damped relative to critical damping, so designers can trade response speed against overshoot and settle the response shape.

People made the laryngocele construct to map the cystic distension of the laryngeal saccule, so that otolaryngologists and head and neck surgeons can diagnose and excise the internal and external neck masses it produces.

People made the terminal-bronchiole construct to map the last purely conducting airway of the tree, so that pathologists mark the conducting-respiratory transition and pulmonologists localize where small-airways disease begins.

People made implicit-memory to classify memory systems that influence behavior without conscious awareness or intentional retrieval, so that cognitive psychologists can distinguish automatic from deliberate memory processes in research and clinical assessment.

People made the esophagus construct to map the muscular conduit connecting the pharynx to the stomach through which ingested material passes, so that clinicians can evaluate swallowing disorders, gastroesophageal reflux, and esophageal neoplasia.
To determine which internal states of a dynamical system can be reconstructed from its measured outputs over time.

People made the pulmonary-artery construct to map the vessels that carry deoxygenated blood from the right ventricle to the lungs for gas exchange, so that radiologists can evaluate pulmonary embolism and surgeons can access the pulmonary vasculature.

People made the hyoid bone construct to map the U-shaped bone in the anterior neck that serves as the primary attachment point for muscles of the tongue, pharynx, and larynx, so that clinicians can identify the key bony landmark for airway manipulation and surgical access in the neck.

People made the alveolus construct to map the microscopic air sac within the lung where gas exchange between air and blood occurs, so that clinicians can diagnose pulmonary gas exchange disorders, understand ventilation-perfusion mismatch, and interpret interstitial lung disease.
To name the single frequency at which a feedback loop's loop gain equals unity, the point at which the phase margin is read and the standard closed-loop bandwidth specification is anchored.

People made the stylohyoid ligament construct to map the band suspending the hyoid bone from the styloid process of the skull, so that anatomists and skull-base surgeons can orient the hyoid suspensions and diagnose its calcifications causing Eagle syndrome.

People made the V/Q mismatch construct to classify patterns of gas-exchange failure where ventilation and perfusion are unevenly distributed across the lung, so that clinicians can diagnose hypoxemia mechanisms and physiologists can predict oxygenation response to supplemental oxygen.

People made the pulmonary-lobule construct to map the smallest structural unit of lung tissue — a polygonal cluster of alveoli and their associated airways supplied by a single terminal bronchiole — so that pathologists can localize disease processes and radiologists can correlate imaging findings with anatomical units.
To specify the time at which a system's response first reaches its maximum value, so designers can quantify how quickly a system responds to transients.

People made the cricopharyngeus-muscle construct to map the tonic sphincter muscle at the pharyngoesophageal junction, so that clinicians can evaluate upper esophageal dysfunction in dysphagia, cricopharyngeal bar, and Zenker's diverticulum.

People made the cricoarytenoid joint construct to map the paired synovial articulation between the arytenoid cartilage and the cricoid cartilage that enables the rotation and sliding which abduct, adduct, and adjust the vocal folds, so that clinicians and voice scientists can understand laryngeal biomechanics relevant to phonation and laryngeal trauma.

A human-made analytical measure separating the amplitude branch of a system's frequency response so that designers can specify, plot, and correct a system's gain behavior across frequency - bandwidth, ripple, roll-off - independently of its phase.
A parameterized family of quadratic time-frequency representations whose kernel function controls the trade-off between cross-term interference and auto-term smoothing.

People made the alveolar-sac construct to map the final gas-exchange saccules that cluster around the respiratory bronchiole, so that histologists can stage emphysema and physiologists can model alveolar surface area.
People made spirometry to provide a quick, noninvasive measurement of lung function, so that clinicians can diagnose obstructive and restrictive airway disease and monitor therapeutic response.
Radar and audio engineers needed a signal whose frequency sweeps predictably over time for target detection and audio synthesis.
To provide optimal state-feedback combined with optimal state estimation when only noisy outputs are available, separating the design into independent LQR and Kalman-filter components.

People made the pulmonary-artery construct to map the arterial vessels that carry deoxygenated blood from the right ventricle to the lungs, so that clinicians can localize pulmonary emboli and surgeons can access these vessels for transplantation or disease intervention.

People made the main-bronchus construct to map each of the two principal airways emerging from the tracheal bifurcation, so that surgeons and radiologists can identify the proximal landmark for lobar-bronchus isolation and bronchopulmonary segment targeting.
To quantify how a feedback system's output tracks reference inputs and rejects measurement noise, as the complementary partner to the sensitivity function.

A nonlinear state estimation algorithm that propagates mean and covariance through a deterministic set of sigma points sampled from the posterior, avoiding Jacobian computation and capturing nonlinearities to at least second-order accuracy.
To quantify the total signal amplification around one pass through a feedback loop, enabling designers to assess stability margins and shape frequency response.

People made the laryngeal-vestibule construct to map the supraglottic chamber between the laryngeal inlet and the vocal folds, so that clinicians can identify its landmarks and its pathologies during laryngoscopy and airway management.

People made the lung construct to map the paired respiratory organs of gas exchange within the thoracic cavity, so that clinicians can diagnose pulmonary disease, interpret chest imaging, and manage respiratory failure.
To shape a system's internal dynamics directly, by computing the control input as a function of the state vector, so that one gain matrix can place the closed-loop poles.

People made the tidal-volume construct to standardize the measurement of air moved per breath, so that clinicians can set mechanical ventilator parameters and physiologists can compute dead-space fractions and minute ventilation.
To reconstruct the full internal state of a linear dynamical system from measured inputs and outputs when not all states are directly observable.

People made the conducting-zone partition to set off the gas-exchanging portion of the airways, so that physiologists can quantify dead space and clinicians can localize where obstruction and resistance arise.
To vary controller parameters as functions of measurable operating conditions so that a single controller design achieves acceptable performance across a wide range of plant behaviors.
To quantify the maximum amplification in a closed-loop system's frequency response, so designers can assess relative stability and predict time-domain ringing.

People made the segmental-bronchus construct to name each airway branch that supplies a single bronchopulmonary segment, so that thoracic surgeons can resect discrete lung units and bronchoscopists can target individual segments.

People made the stomach construct to map the muscular organ that receives ingested food from the esophagus, stores and mixes it with gastric secretions, and begins protein digestion, so that clinicians can evaluate dyspepsia, peptic ulcer disease, and gastric neoplasia.

People made the pulmonary-artery construct to map the deoxygenated arterial pathway from the right ventricle to the pulmonary capillary beds, so that cardiologists, anesthesiologists, and vascular surgeons can assess pulmonary hypertension and plan catheter and surgical interventions.

People made the bronchiole construct to map the cartilage-free airway segment distal to the segmental bronchi, so that histology, physiology and clinical practice can mark the conducting-respiratory boundary and categorize small-airways disease.
A human-made normalization procedure applied to cepstral coefficients to remove artifacts from recording conditions and channel effects, making coefficients comparable across speakers and sessions.

People made the laryngeal saccule construct to map the blind mucosal pouch of the laryngeal ventricle so that clinicians can diagnose laryngoceles and understand the route of lubricant delivery to the vocal fold mucosa.

People made the palatine-tonsil construct to map the paired lymphoid tissue masses embedded in the lateral walls of the oropharynx, so that clinicians can diagnose tonsillitis, distinguish normal lymphoid tissue from neoplasia, and plan tonsillectomy.

People made the alveolar-capillary membrane construct to map the thin diffusion barrier between alveolar air and pulmonary capillary blood, so that physiologists can model gas exchange, pathologists can assess interstitial lung disease, and clinicians can interpret diffusing capacity measurements.

A human-made spectral representation that estimates the cross-frequency relationship between two signals by normalizing their cross-spectrum by the product of their individual power spectral densities, enabling transfer-function estimation and coherence analysis.

People made the bronchial-tree construct to map the hierarchical branching pattern of conducting airways from the tracheal bifurcation to the terminal respiratory units, so that clinicians can navigate the bronchial tree during bronchoscopy and surgeons can plan resections by segment.

A nonlinear state estimation algorithm that linearizes the system's nonlinear state-transition and observation models around the current estimate using Jacobian matrices, extending the linear Kalman filter to handle smooth nonlinear dynamics.

People made the pulmonary-vein construct to map the vessels that return oxygenated blood from the lungs to the left atrium, so that radiologists and surgeons can evaluate pulmonary venous anomalies and plan cardiac interventions.

People made the trachea construct to map and categorize the cartilaginous tubular airway connecting the larynx to the bronchi, so that clinicians can manage the airway, perform tracheostomy, and diagnose airway pathology.
A spectral representation quantifying the frequency-domain relationship between two signals, computed as the conjugate product of their individual spectra.

People made the functional-residual-capacity construct to define the lung volume remaining after passive exhalation, so that clinicians can interpret body-plethysmography results and physiologists can compute the alveolar gas composition at end-expiration.

To provide a formal criterion for whether a system's inputs can steer its internal state to any desired value, so engineers can verify that control design is structurally feasible before investing in gain tuning.

People made the hyoepiglottic-ligament construct to map the fibrous connection between the hyoid bone and the epiglottis, so that surgeons and airway clinicians can identify this landmark during laryngeal surgery and neck dissection.
To visualize how a system's closed-loop poles move in the complex plane as a gain parameter varies, enabling designers to select gain for desired stability and transient response.

People made the hyoid bone construct to map the suspended U-shaped bone above the larynx, so that clinicians can orient the laryngeal framework and read its fractures as a marker of blunt neck trauma.

Anatomical construct delineating the middle division of the pharynx, lying behind the oral cavity and above the epiglottis, serving as the shared passage where air and food converge before diverging into the respiratory and digestive tracts.

People made the alveolar-duct construct to map the thin-walled gas-exchanging airways that follow the respiratory bronchioles and open into the alveolar sacs, so that histologists and physiologists can trace the transition from the conducting airway to the gas-exchange unit within the pulmonary acinus.

People made the pulmonary-hilum construct to map the medial entry-and-exit zone of each lung where its bronchus, vessels, and nerves enter and exit, so that radiologists can stage hilar and mediastinal lymph nodes and thoracic surgeons can plan hilar dissection.

To express the feedback system's effective input-output behavior as a single transfer function once the feedback path is included, so designers can analyze stability and response from the loop rather than from its parts.
A human-made audio signal processing technique for time-scale modification using the phase vocoder architecture.

People made the internal-laryngeal-nerve construct to map the sensory branch of the superior laryngeal nerve that pierces the thyrohyoid membrane, so that clinicians can perform targeted regional anesthesia and identify the nerve during thyroid and laryngeal surgery.

The inverse Fourier transform is a human-made mathematical operation that reconstructs a time-domain function or discrete sequence from its frequency-domain representation by inverting the Fourier transform decomposition.
To quantify the worst-case effect of structured plant uncertainty on closed-loop stability and performance, generalizing the singular value to account for specific uncertainty patterns.

People made the thyrohyoid membrane construct to map the fibrous sheet connecting the hyoid bone to the thyroid cartilage, so that clinicians can identify the superior boundary of the anterior laryngeal wall and navigate surgical approaches in the suprahyoid neck.

A human-made analytical measure of the time delay experienced by the phase of an individual frequency component as it passes through a system, used to characterize phase linearity in filter design and communications.
A human-made time-frequency analysis method that computes a signal's spectral content using a Gaussian window, yielding an optimally localized representation in the time-frequency plane.

People made the segmental-bronchus construct to map each named airway branch arising from a lobar bronchus that supplies a single bronchopulmonary segment, so that thoracic surgeons can resect individual segments and bronchoscopists can target localized airway disease.

People made the vocal ligament construct to map and categorize the elastic fiber band that forms the core of the vocal fold, so that clinicians can identify its structural role in phonation and recognize its injury during laryngeal surgery.

People made the phrenic-nerve construct to map the paired nerve (C3-C5) that supplies the diaphragm and the pericardial and pleural pleurae, so that clinicians can localize diaphragmatic paralysis, phrenic nerve injury, and the referred shoulder-tip pain of diaphragmatic irritation.
People made the tracheal-cartilage construct to map the C-shaped hyaline rings that keep the tracheal lumen patent, so that clinicians can plan tracheostomy, resection, and airway reconstruction.

People made the inferior-pharyngeal-constrictor construct to map the lowest pharyngeal constrictor muscle band arising from the cricoid and thyroid cartilages, enabling clinicians to assess swallowing disorders and cricopharyngeal dysfunction.
To combine state estimation and state-feedback into a single implementable control law, using estimated states for real-time control.
People made the lower-airway category to name the distal segment of the respiratory airway, so that clinicians can localize airway disease and distinguish it from upper-airway obstruction.
To permit independent design of a state observer and a state-feedback controller, then combine them while preserving the eigenvalue structure of both.

People made the subsegmental-bronchus construct to map the airway level between the segmental bronchi and the cartilage-free bronchioles, so that bronchoscopists can navigate the last cartilage-bearing generation and histologists can mark the bronchial-bronchiolar transition.
To improve a feedback system's steady-state accuracy by increasing low-frequency gain without significantly reducing stability margins.

A state-space factorization of a linear plant P(s) into four stable transfer function matrices satisfying the Bézout identity. Enables Youla parametrization and H-infinity synthesis. Persisted in MATLAB Robust Control Toolbox and control theory textbooks.
To specify the time required for a system's transient response to decay within a defined tolerance band around its final value, so designers can quantify response speed.

A human-made interval of the frequency axis bounding a portion of a signal's spectrum, made so that analysis, filtering, and gain can be applied to a band-limited part of a signal instead of the whole.

People made the paraglottic space construct to map the fat-filled lateral compartment of the larynx, so that radiologists and head and neck surgeons can assess tumor spread in laryngeal cancer staging and plan surgical approaches.
A discrete frequency index in a spectral decomposition, representing a narrow band of frequencies at a specific center frequency.
To specify the frequency at which an undamped second-order system would oscillate freely, so designers can quantify the inherent oscillatory timescale of a system.

People made the airway construct to map the passages conducting air from the external environment to the gas-exchange surfaces of the lung parenchyma, so that clinicians and physiologists can categorize airway diseases by anatomical level and plan airway management interventions.

People made the terminal-bronchiole construct to map the most distal purely conducting airway, so that histologists can identify the boundary between conducting and respiratory zones and clinicians can assess small-airways disease.

People made the pulmonary-capillary construct to identify the capillary segments that interface with alveolar air for gas exchange, so that physiologists can compute diffusion capacities and clinicians can assess ventilation-perfusion matching.

People made the main-bronchus construct to name the two primary airway passages at the tracheal bifurcation, so that clinicians can distinguish the right and left airways for bronchoscopy, surgery, and aspiration management.
People made the cricotracheal membrane attachment construct to map the inferior cricoid to first tracheal ring junction for surgical landmarking during airway procedures.

Made so that a signal can be analyzed, specified, and measured by its moment-by-moment values in time instead of by its frequency content, giving the discipline a boundary - the time-versus-frequency split - that its curricula, standards, and instruments keep in daily use.
To quantify the phase shift a system introduces between input and output signals at a given frequency, so engineers can budget phase margin and assess stability margins in feedback designs.

A mathematical construction in robust control that parameterizes the set of all stabilizing controllers for a linear plant using a stable free parameter Q. Enables systematic synthesis of optimal controllers via convex optimization over the Youla parameter. Persisted in control theory textbooks and robust control software toolboxes.

People made the vital-capacity construct to measure the maximum volume of air a person can expel from the lungs after a maximal inhalation, so that clinicians can classify obstructive and restrictive ventilatory defects and track pulmonary disease progression.

People made the diaphragm construct to map the dome-shaped muscle separating the thoracic and abdominal cavities, which drives breathing and transmits pressure between them, so that clinicians can evaluate diaphragmatic dysfunction, herniation, and the passage of vessels and the esophagus through it.

A convex constraint in robust control and optimization where a symmetric matrix, linear in decision variables, must be positive or negative semidefinite. Serves as the unifying computational framework for H-infinity control, pole placement, and robust stability analysis, replacing non-convex Riccati equations with tractable convex feasibility problems. Persisted in YALMPI, SeDuMi, Mosek, and SDPT4 solvers.

To express a feedback system's stability margin as the extra pure time delay the loop can absorb before it reaches the stability boundary, so designers with sensors, actuators, or network latency can budget how much delay is safe.

People made the vallecula construct to map the shallow depression between the base of the tongue and the epiglottis, so that clinicians can assess airway patency during laryngoscopy and identify pathology in this common site of cyst formation.
To provide a relaxed controllability criterion that allows uncontrollable modes when they are naturally stable, enabling practical controller design for systems that are not fully controllable.

To read a system's stability margins, bandwidth, and phase behavior directly from a straight-line-approximable log-log rendering of its frequency response, so designers can assess and correct phase and gain without solving the closed-loop equations.

People made the lingual-tonsil construct to map the collection of lymphoid tissue at the posterior third of the tongue base, so that clinicians can assess lingual tonsillar hypertrophy causing obstructive sleep apnea, plan lingual tonsillectomy, and distinguish lingual tonsil tissue from base-of-tongue neoplasia.

People made the artery construct to map blood vessels that carry blood away from the heart, providing the high-pressure conduit system that delivers oxygenated blood to tissues or deoxygenated blood to the lungs.

People made the thyrohyoid membrane construct to map the fibrous band joining the thyroid cartilage to the hyoid bone, so that clinicians can orient the laryngeal framework and reach the larynx in surgery.

People made the right-main-bronchus construct to name the wider, shorter, more vertical primary airway entering the right lung, so that surgeons and bronchoscopists can navigate the asymmetric airway and clinicians can manage aspiration.

People made the pharynx construct to map the muscular tube connecting the nasal and oral cavities to the larynx and esophagus, so that clinicians can localize lesions, plan surgical approaches, and manage airway obstruction at the crossroads of the respiratory and digestive tracts.
A quadratic time-frequency representation that maps signal energy onto the time-frequency plane with exact marginal properties.
To estimate the internal state of a system from its outputs, enabling state-feedback control when full state measurement is unavailable.

People made the conus elasticus construct to map the conical fibrous membrane connecting the cricoid cartilage to the thyroid cartilage and vocal ligaments, so that clinicians can understand the structural continuity of the laryngeal framework and the pathway for the internal laryngeal nerve.

People made the trachealis-muscle construct to map the smooth muscle closing the posterior gap of the tracheal cartilages, so that clinicians can understand tracheal dynamics during respiration and manage airway obstruction.
To provide a linear matrix equation whose solvability characterizes asymptotic stability of linear dynamical systems, forming the algebraic backbone of Lyapunov stability theory.

Anatomical construct delineating the superior division of the pharynx, lying behind the nasal cavity and above the soft palate, serving as the shared passage for air before it diverges into the larynx and esophagus.
To quantify how quickly a system's transient response reaches its target value for the first time, so designers can evaluate transient speed.

People made the peak expiratory flow construct to map the maximum speed of exhalation from full lung inflation, so that clinicians can quickly screen for obstructive airway disease and monitor asthma severity at the bedside.

People made the respiratory-zone partition to set off the gas-exchanging portion of the airways, so that physiologists can locate where oxygen and carbon dioxide cross and model the gas-exchange surface.
People made the small-airways category to name the distal airways below the cartilage-bearing bronchi, so that clinicians can detect early obstructive disease before it reaches the large airways.

People made the segmental-bronchus construct to map each airway branch that enters a specific bronchopulmonary segment of a lung, so that surgeons can perform segmental resections and radiologists can localize segmental consolidations.
A classification map drawn by time-frequency analysts to group bilinear representations that share kernel parameterization and cross-term interference behavior.

People made the lung-compliance construct to quantify the pressure-volume relationship of the lung, so that clinicians can classify restrictive versus obstructive disease and physiologists can model respiratory mechanics.
To provide a relaxed observability criterion that allows unobservable modes when they are naturally stable, enabling practical state-observer design for systems that are not fully observable.
Anatomical construct identifying the paired conical cartilages sitting atop the apices of the arytenoid cartilages in the larynx, contributing to the posterior aspect of the laryngeal inlet.
People made the flow-volume curve construct to provide a visual representation of lung mechanics, so that clinicians can distinguish obstructive from restrictive disease patterns at a glance.

People made the cricothyroid membrane construct to map the fibrous sheet between the thyroid and cricoid cartilages, so that clinicians can identify the emergency airway landmark and the vocal ligament's relationship to the airway wall.

To provide a nonlinear matrix equation whose solution yields optimal feedback gains for linear systems with quadratic cost, and whose stability characterizations underpin Lyapunov theory in control and estimation.

People made the pleura construct to map the double-layered serous membrane enclosing the lungs and lining the thoracic cavity, so that clinicians can diagnose pleural disease, interpret chest imaging, and manage pleural effusions.

Made so that a signal can be analyzed, specified, and measured by the amplitudes and phases of its frequency components instead of by its waveform, giving the discipline a boundary - the frequency-versus-time split - that its curricula, standards, and instruments keep in daily use.

A human-made dimensionless quantity between 0 and 1 that quantifies the linear relationship between two signals at each frequency, computed as the squared magnitude of the cross-spectral density divided by the product of their individual power spectral densities.
To visualize a system's open-loop frequency response in the complex plane, revealing stability margins through encirclement patterns around the critical point.
To shape the loop gain frequency response across bandwidth so that closed-loop systems meet robustness and performance specifications through frequency-domain design.

Made so that the phase relationship between two signals can be measured and used separately from the magnitudes of their cross-spectral density, for delay estimation, phase-based coupling analysis, and phase consistency checks in system identification.
To let designers read a feedback system's closed-loop gain and stability directly from its open-loop frequency response, without recomputing the closed loop at every gain.
A human-made representation of a signal or function parameterized by time, where the signal's value at each point on the time axis encodes its state.

A robust control design methodology that synthesizes a controller to minimize the worst-case gain of the closed-loop system from disturbances to controlled outputs. Uses state-space methods to achieve guaranteed performance and stability margins. Persisted in aerospace guidance, robotics, and process control toolboxes.

People made the hypopharynx construct to map the inferior portion of the pharynx behind the larynx, so that clinicians can localize and stage cancers, assess swallowing dysfunction, and plan surgical reconstruction of the aerodigestive junction.

To decide whether a feedback system is stable without solving the closed-loop characteristic equation: count how many times the open-loop response encircles the critical point and compare that count with the open-loop unstable poles, so designers can settle stability from the loop response alone.

People made the postcricoid region construct to map the hypopharyngeal subsite behind the cricoid cartilage so that clinicians can localize cancers, assess swallowing pathology, and plan esophageal surgery.

People made the cuneiform cartilage construct to map and categorize the paired nodular elastic cartilages embedded within the aryepiglottic folds, so that clinicians can identify their variable presence during laryngoscopy and recognize them as anatomical landmarks during head and neck surgery.

People made the surfactant construct to categorize the surface-active lipid-protein mixture that reduces alveolar surface tension, so that neonatologists can diagnose respiratory distress and clinicians can replace deficient surfactant.

People made the alveolar-capillary membrane construct to name the diffusion barrier between alveolar air and capillary blood, so that physiologists can compute the lung's diffusing capacity and clinicians can separate membrane limitation from perfusion limitation in gas-exchange failure.
To specify the maximum amount by which a system's response exceeds its final steady-state value, so designers can quantify transient quality and stability margin.

People made the bronchial-artery construct to map the systemic arterial supply that carries oxygenated blood from the aorta to the bronchi and lung, so that interventional radiologists can embolize the source of massive hemoptysis and surgeons can control the bronchial circulation.
People made the laryngeal surgical landmark construct to map the physical sites in the larynx used as reference points during airway surgery.
A human-made signal-processing procedure that reconstructs a time-domain signal from a short-time Fourier (STFT) decomposition by frame-wise inverse transform and overlap-and-add synthesis.

People made the stylopharyngeus muscle construct to map the unique longitudinal pharyngeal muscle that elevates the pharynx and larynx during swallowing so that clinicians can assess cranial nerve IX function, plan pharyngeal surgery, and evaluate swallowing disorders.
To improve a feedback system's phase margin and transient response speed by adding positive phase shift near the crossover frequency.

People made the endotracheal tube to keep the airway patent during general anesthesia and mechanical ventilation, so that a patient whose airway is unprotected or obstructed can be ventilated and protected from aspiration.
To measure how far a spectral estimate is from the original spectrum with a divergence matched to log-spectra, so cepstral feature pipelines can be scored against the true spectrum.
To compute optimal state-feedback control by minimizing a weighted quadratic cost, balancing state regulation against control effort, producing gains that guarantee stability margins and robustness.

People made the vein construct to map blood vessels that carry blood toward the heart, providing the low-pressure return conduit that collects deoxygenated blood from tissues or oxygenated blood from the lungs back to the heart.
To quantify the rate at which a system's gain falls off beyond its passband, so engineers can predict attenuation of out-of-band signals and design adequate filter selectivity.
To achieve robust tracking and disturbance rejection in nonlinear systems by driving states to a switching surface and maintaining sliding motion despite model uncertainty.

People made the cricotracheal membrane construct to map the fibrous connective tissue bridging the cricoid cartilage to the first tracheal ring, so that clinicians can identify this surgical landmark during airway procedures.

People made the thyroepiglottic-ligament construct to map the fibrous connection between the epiglottis and the thyroid cartilage, so that laryngeal surgeons and airway clinicians can identify this landmark during surgical procedures and intubation.

People made the bronchiole construct to map the cartilage-free segment of the bronchial tree distal to the segmental bronchi, so that pathologists can identify the conducting-respiratory boundary and pulmonologists can categorize small-airways disease.

People made the terminal-bronchiole construct to map the last conducting airway generation before gas exchange begins, so that pathologists and physiologists can define the boundary between the conducting and respiratory zones of the lung.

Anatomists and airway surgeons needed a single stable name for the complete cartilaginous scaffold of the larynx, because laryngofissure, shunt surgery, and total laryngectomy are planned around the whole scaffold and its inter-cartilaginous joints, not around individual cartilages.

People made the left-main-bronchus construct to name the narrower, longer, more horizontal primary airway entering the left lung, so that clinicians can distinguish left from right airway anatomy for bronchoscopy, aspiration management, and surgical planning.

People made the bronchopulmonary-segment construct to map each discrete anatomic unit of a lobe that carries its own segmental bronchus and bronchial arterial branch, so that surgeons can plan segmentectomy and radiologists can localize disease to a named segment.

People made the rima glottidis construct to map and categorize the slit-like space between the vocal folds within the glottis, so that clinicians can identify its dimensions during airway management and assess vocal fold mobility.
A human-made representational space needed to analyze signals in terms of their constituent frequencies rather than their temporal evolution.

People made the alveolar-capillary-membrane construct to identify the diffusion barrier between alveolar air and pulmonary capillary blood, so that physiologists can compute gas exchange and pathologists can assess thickening in disease.
Made so that a processed frequency representation can be returned to the time domain: the reciprocal step that closes the DFT pair and makes spectral processing reversible.

People made the pharyngeal recess construct to map the depression in the superior-posterior nasopharynx so that clinicians can identify the most common site of nasopharyngeal carcinoma origin, assess nasopharyngeal disease, and plan oncological treatment.

People made the pulmonary-acinus construct to map the functional gas-exchange unit of the lung distal to a terminal bronchiole, so that physiologists can quantify surface area, pathologists can grade emphysema, and clinicians can understand regional ventilation patterns.

People made the segmental-bronchus construct to map each named airway branch arising from a lobar bronchus and supplying a single bronchopulmonary segment, so that thoracic surgeons can perform segmentectomy and bronchoscopists can localize disease to a specific lobar region.

People made the anatomical dead space construct to quantify the ventilatory volume that does not participate in gas exchange, so that clinicians can compute alveolar ventilation and adjust mechanical ventilation settings.
The complete frequency-domain representation of a signal as complex-valued coefficients encoding both amplitude and phase at each frequency, obtained via spectral decomposition.
People made the upper-airway category to name the proximal segment of the respiratory airway, so that clinicians can localize the site of airway obstruction and anticipate the difficult airway.
To compute the state-feedback gain matrix for single-input systems that places closed-loop poles at specified locations by solving for the unique gain using the controllable canonical form.

People made the spirometry construct to map the measurement of lung volumes and flows during breathing, so that clinicians can diagnose obstructive and restrictive lung disease, monitor disease progression, and assess treatment response.
To quantify a system's stability by measuring the gain difference from 0 dB at the frequency where phase reaches -180 degrees, giving engineers a margin for gain increase before instability occurs.

To identify the complex-plane locations where a system's transfer function becomes infinite or zero, determining its stability and dynamic behavior, so engineers can analyze, place, and shape system response through pole-zero design.
To reject a narrow band of unwanted frequencies from a signal while passing all other frequencies with minimal distortion.

People made the superior laryngeal nerve construct to map and categorize the branch of the vagus nerve that supplies sensory and motor innervation to the larynx above the vocal folds, so that clinicians can perform regional anesthesia and recognize nerve injury during thyroid and laryngeal surgery.

People made the nasal-cavity construct to map the paired air-filled space within the skull that warms, humidifies and filters the inspired air, so that otolaryngologists can localize the conchae, the meatuses and the sinus openings during rhinoscopy and endoscopic sinus surgery.

People made the intermediate-tracheal ligament construct to map the anterior fibrous band connecting the cricoid cartilage to the first tracheal ring, so that surgeons can identify this landmark during tracheostomy and laryngotracheal surgery.
To synthesize controllers that guarantee stability and performance margins in the presence of bounded plant uncertainty by minimizing worst-case disturbance-to-output gain.

People made the terminal-bronchiole construct to map the last purely conducting airway before the respiratory zone begins, so that pathologists can identify the conducting-respiratory transition and clinicians can localize small-airways disease.

People made the salpingopharyngeus muscle construct to map the longitudinal pharyngeal muscle that elevates the pharynx from the auditory tube origin so that clinicians can assess swallowing function, evaluate nasopharyngeal disease, and plan head-and-neck surgery.
To design controllers that ensure robust performance against structured uncertainty by minimizing the structured singular value (mu) of the closed-loop system.
To quantify a system's stability by measuring the phase difference from -180 degrees at the frequency where gain crosses unity, giving engineers a margin for phase lag before instability occurs.

People made the bronchiole construct to map the small-caliber cartilage-free airways branching from the main bronchi down to the terminal bronchioles, so that clinicians can understand the conducting zone of the lung, diagnose obstructive airway diseases, and interpret the site of aerosol drug deposition.

People made the superior-pharyngeal-constrictor construct to map the uppermost pharyngeal constrictor muscle band that forms the posterior and lateral walls of the superior pharynx, enabling clinicians to localize pharyngeal constriction defects and retropharyngeal abscesses.

People made the mucociliary escalator construct to map the coordinated mucus-and-cilia mechanism that clears the airway, so that pulmonologists can quantify its dysfunction in diseases like primary ciliary dyskinesia and chronic bronchitis.

People made the respiratory bronchiole construct to map the transitional airway between conducting bronchioles and alveolar ducts, where sparse alveoli appear in its wall and limited gas exchange begins, so that pathologists can identify the respiratory zone and clinicians can localize the site of early smoke-induced parenchymal damage.

People made the forced vital capacity construct to map the total volume of air that can be forcibly exhaled after a maximal inhalation, so that clinicians can quantify restrictive ventilatory defects and track disease progression in interstitial lung disease.

To design controllers for plants whose exact dynamics are unknown within a norm-bounded set, guaranteeing performance and stability against the worst admissible plant rather than the nominal one, where a single mean-square optimum (LQR) cannot certify robustness.

People made the bronchiole construct to map the terminal airway branches within the lung parenchyma distal to the bronchi, so that clinicians can diagnose bronchiolar disease, understand airflow regulation, and interpret pulmonary pathology.

People made the pulmonary-acinus construct to give a single name to the lung unit bounded by one terminal bronchiole, so that pathologists can locate emphysema and other acinar diseases and radiologists can read the unit on imaging.
To quantify the residual difference between a system's final output and its desired target after transients have decayed, so designers can assess long-term accuracy.

To enforce constraints on inputs, states, and outputs in real-time control by repeatedly solving a finite-horizon optimization over a prediction model and applying only the first computed control move.

People made the bronchiole construct to map the small cartilage-free conducting airways that convey air from the bronchial tree to the respiratory zone, so that pulmonologists can localize small-airway disease and interpret bronchial conductive resistance.
